summary: Defines the Encapsulating Security Payload, a header that can provide confidentiality, data origin authentication and replay protection for IPv4 and IPv6 packets. It is the part of IPsec that actually encrypts traffic. It was replaced by RFC 4303 and RFC 4305.

plainLanguage.summary: ESP is the IPsec header that does the actual protecting. It sits after the IP header, carries the packet's contents in an encrypted form when encryption is wanted, and adds a code that lets the receiver check that nothing was changed and that the packet is not a copy of an earlier one.

questions: what is the encapsulating security payload
what is the esp header format
what is the difference between transport and tunnel mode
subtitle: The IPsec header that encrypts and authenticates the traffic it carries.

tldr.problem: IP traffic crosses networks that cannot be trusted, so packets need to be protected. The protection has to work in IPv4 and IPv6, and it has to fit inside the IP header without changing how the network carries the packet.
tldr.mechanism: ESP adds a header after the IP header that holds a security association identifier, a sequence number, the protected payload, padding and an integrity check value. The payload can be encrypted, and the whole packet can be signed, with the choice made when the security association is set up.
tldr.outcome: The RFC also fixes the processing rules for sending and receiving, including a sliding window that rejects replayed packets. It replaced RFC 1827 and was later obsoleted by RFC 4303 and RFC 4305.

today: RFC 2406 is a Proposed Standard that replaced RFC 1827 and was itself obsoleted by RFC 4303 and RFC 4305.

sections.title: What ESP Provides
sections.content:
The Encapsulating Security Payload header is designed to provide a mix of security services in IPv4 and IPv6. ESP may be applied on its own, in combination with the IP Authentication Header, or nested, for example through the use of tunnel mode. The services can be provided between a pair of communicating hosts, between a pair of communicating security gateways, or between a security gateway and a host.

ESP is used to provide confidentiality, data origin authentication, connectionless integrity, an anti-replay service, which is a form of partial sequence integrity, and limited traffic flow confidentiality. Which services are provided depends on the options selected when the security association is established and on where the implementation sits.

Confidentiality may be selected on its own. However, using confidentiality without integrity or authentication, whether from ESP or from a separate AH, exposes the traffic to certain forms of active attack that could undermine the confidentiality service. Data origin authentication and connectionless integrity are joint services, referred to together as authentication, and are offered as an option together with the optional confidentiality.

The anti-replay service may be selected only if data origin authentication is selected, and choosing it is solely at the discretion of the receiver. The default calls for the sender to increment the sequence number used for anti-replay, but the service is effective only if the receiver checks that number. Traffic flow confidentiality requires tunnel mode and is most effective when implemented at a security gateway, where traffic aggregation may be able to mask true source and destination patterns. Although both confidentiality and authentication are optional, at least one of them must be selected.

The protocol header that immediately precedes the ESP header contains the value 50 in its Protocol field for IPv4, or its Next Header field for IPv6 and extension headers.
sections.plainLanguage: ESP can hide the contents of a packet, prove who sent it, show that it was not altered, and make sure the receiver does not accept the same packet twice. Each of those is switched on separately when the connection is set up.

sections.title: The ESP Header
sections.content:
The Security Parameters Index is an arbitrary 32-bit value that, together with the destination IP address and the security protocol, uniquely identifies the security association for the datagram. The values from 1 through 255 are reserved by IANA for future use, and the value zero is reserved for local, implementation-specific use and must not be sent on the wire. The field is ordinarily chosen by the destination system when the association is established.

The Sequence Number is an unsigned 32-bit counter that increases monotonically. It is mandatory and always present, even if the receiver does not enable the anti-replay service. The sender's and the receiver's counters start at zero when the association is established, so the first packet has a sequence number of 1. If anti-replay is enabled, which is the default, the number must never cycle, so the counters must be reset by establishing a new association and a new key before the 2^32nd packet is sent.

Payload Data is a variable-length field holding the data described by the next header field. If the encryption algorithm needs cryptographic synchronisation data, such as an initialisation vector, that data may be carried explicitly in this field. An algorithm that needs such data must state its length, structure and location in the RFC that defines its use with ESP.

Padding exists for several reasons. It fills the plaintext to a multiple of the cipher's block size, and it makes sure the pad length and next header fields are right-aligned within a four-byte word, so that the authentication data is aligned on a four-byte boundary. Extra padding beyond those needs may be used to conceal the real length of the payload, which helps with traffic flow confidentiality, but it costs bandwidth. The sender may add 0 to 255 bytes of padding, and all implementations must support generating and consuming it. Where padding is needed and the algorithm does not specify its contents, the default is a series of unsigned one-byte integers counting up from 1.

The Pad Length says how many padding bytes immediately precede it, from 0 to 255. The Next Header is an 8-bit field saying what the payload holds, for example an extension header in IPv6 or an upper layer protocol identifier. Authentication Data holds the integrity check value, computed over the ESP packet minus the authentication data itself. It is present only when the authentication service has been selected for the association, and its length is set by the authentication algorithm.
sections.plainLanguage: The header names which set of keys is in use and carries a counter that goes up by one on every packet. It then holds the protected data, some padding so the cipher and the signature line up, a field saying what the data is, and finally the code that proves nothing was tampered with.

sections.title: Transport Mode and Tunnel Mode
sections.content:
ESP may be employed in two ways, transport mode or tunnel mode.

In transport mode the ESP header is inserted after the IP header and before the upper layer protocol header, and it protects the upper layer protocol information but not the IP header. The mode is applicable only to host implementations. The RFC notes that the word transport should not be misconstrued as restricting the mode to TCP and UDP, and that an ICMP message may be sent using either transport mode or tunnel mode. In IPv4 this means placing ESP after the IP header and any options it contains, but before the upper layer protocol.

In tunnel mode ESP protects the entire inner IP packet, including the entire inner IP header. The outer IP header may hold different addresses, for example the addresses of security gateways. Tunnel mode may be used by hosts or by security gateways, and a gateway protecting subscriber transit traffic must use it. The position of ESP relative to the outer IP header is the same as in transport mode.

ESP and AH headers can be combined in a variety of modes, and the IPsec Architecture document describes which combinations of security associations must be supported.
sections.plainLanguage: Transport mode protects the contents of a packet but leaves its IP address visible. Tunnel mode wraps the whole packet, original address and all, inside a new one, so the address the packet came from is hidden.

sections.title: Sending and Receiving Packets
sections.content:
On the way out, the sender looks up the security association for the packet and then encapsulates the upper layer protocol information in the ESP header in transport mode, or the entire original IP datagram in tunnel mode. It adds any necessary padding, and then encrypts the payload data, padding, pad length and next header using the key, algorithm and mode the association names. If the algorithm needs explicit synchronisation data such as an initialisation vector, that is fed to the algorithm and placed in the payload field; if the data is implicit, the algorithm constructs it.

If authentication is selected, encryption is performed first, and the encryption does not cover the authentication data field. This order lets the receiver reject replayed or bogus packets before doing the expensive decryption, which reduces the impact of denial of service attacks, and it lets the receiver decrypt and verify in parallel. Because the authentication data is not protected by the encryption, a keyed authentication algorithm must be used to compute the integrity check value.

The sender's counter starts at zero when the association is established and is incremented for each packet, so the first packet has a sequence number of 1. If anti-replay is enabled the sender must not send a packet that would make the number cycle, and an attempt to do so is an auditable event.

On the way in, the receiver reassembles the packet if needed, looks up the association using the destination address, the protocol and the SPI, and checks the sequence number. If no valid association exists, the packet is discarded, and that is an auditable event. The SA says whether the sequence number will be checked, whether the authentication data should be present, and which algorithms and keys to use.

All ESP implementations must support the anti-replay service, though the receiver may enable or disable it for each association. It must not be enabled unless authentication is also enabled, because otherwise the sequence number is not protected. If the receiver has enabled it, the receive counter starts at zero when the association is established, and each packet must carry a sequence number that has not already been seen in the life of that association. Duplicates are rejected with a sliding receive window. A minimum window size of 32 must be supported, and a size of 64 is preferred and should be the default. Packets below the left edge of the window are rejected, packets inside it are checked against the list of received packets, and the window is updated only if the integrity check passes.

If the computed and received integrity check values match, the datagram is valid and accepted. If the test fails, the receiver must discard the datagram as invalid, and that is an auditable event. Decryption then removes the outer header and reconstructs the original datagram, whether that is the original IP header plus the upper layer information, or the tunnel IP header plus the whole original datagram.

Fragmentation is performed after ESP processing, so transport mode ESP is applied only to whole IP datagrams. A packet offered to ESP that still looks like an IP fragment must be discarded by the receiver, and that is an auditable event.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender hides the data first and then signs what it produced, so that a receiver can throw a bad packet away before doing the hard work. The receiver checks the counter against a window of recent numbers, so an old copy of a packet is refused, and then checks the signature before opening the packet.

sections.title: Security Considerations, Auditing and Conformance
sections.content:
The RFC says that security is central to the design of the protocol, so security considerations permeate the specification, and that additional aspects of using IPsec are discussed in the Security Architecture document.

Not every system that implements ESP will implement auditing, but if ESP is incorporated into a system that supports auditing then the ESP implementation must also support it, and a system administrator must be able to enable or disable auditing for ESP. Several auditable events are identified in the specification, and for each of them a minimum set of information should be included in the log, such as the SPI value, the date and time received, the source and destination addresses, the sequence number and, in IPv6, the flow ID. There is no requirement for the receiver to send any message to the purported sender when it detects an auditable event, because of the potential to induce a denial of service by doing so.

Implementations claiming conformance must implement the ESP syntax and processing described in the RFC and must comply with all the requirements of the Security Architecture document. If the key used to compute the integrity check value is manually distributed, correct provision of the anti-replay service would need the sender to maintain its counter state carefully until the key is replaced, and there would likely be no automated recovery if the counter were about to overflow, so a compliant implementation should not provide that service for manually keyed associations.

A compliant implementation must support DES in CBC mode for encryption, HMAC with MD5 and HMAC with SHA-1 for authentication, and the NULL authentication and NULL encryption algorithms. The two NULL algorithms are needed because both services are optional, and the way they are negotiated has to stay consistent. While authentication and encryption can each be NULL, they must not both be NULL.
sections.plainLanguage: Some things that go wrong have to be recorded, such as a packet that failed its integrity check, so that an administrator can see them. The RFC also lists the algorithms every implementation must be able to do, including the old ones, because the format was fixed in 1998.

viz.caption: The fields of the ESP header

items.title: Security Parameters Index
items.text: A 32-bit value that, with the destination address and the protocol, identifies the security association.

items.title: Sequence Number
items.text: A 32-bit counter that rises with every packet. It is always present, even when anti-replay is not used.

items.title: Payload Data
items.text: The data being protected, and possibly an initialisation vector. In tunnel mode it holds the whole original datagram.

items.title: Padding
items.text: Zero to 255 bytes, used to line the data up for the cipher and to make the real length of the payload less obvious.

items.title: Pad Length
items.text: How many padding bytes immediately precede it, from 0 to 255.

items.title: Next Header
items.text: An 8-bit field saying what the payload holds, such as an upper layer protocol number.

items.title: Authentication Data
items.text: The integrity check value, present only when the association asked for authentication.
